rv.q: This Christmas Carol will send you out into the cold feeling warm, reflective, and maybe — maybe — just a little less cynical about the state of the world right now.
This 'Christmas Carol' is a lavish, old-fashioned spectacle that delivers the holiday goods with impressive technical wizardry and heartfelt performances.
Mays, of course, is a superb actor — as honest as Bob Cratchit, as direct as the Ghost of Christmas Past, as unflinching as the spirt with the specters of the future.
This “Carol” is a breathless entertainment.

For all its dizzying charms, the overstuffed show doesn’t quite deliver on what really counts — the three Spirits of Christmas Past, Christmas Present and Christmas Future, as they conjure up visions to terrify Scrooge into changing his parsimonious ways.
Even if you’re a Scrooge when it comes to annual holiday fare, like I am, “A Christmas Carol” succeeds as a strong piece of theater.
As in that show, he is a whirling wonder here, in a skillful if sometimes overly dense adaptation he wrote alongside the production’s director, Michael Arden, and Susan Lyons.
As luxurious and theatrically adventurous as “A Christmas Carol” is, there is no substitute for purpose.

The show isn’t flawless — there’s an audience participation section that feels underbaked, and I question the choice of a venue like the Armory, with its patina of wealth and its solid block of well-dressed audience members seated facing the action but well apart from it.
Having prepared his version for some time, he’s now brought it to Broadway – and magnificently.
The narrative is gripping, Mr. Mays’s storytelling talent is formidable, and the production values are sensational.
It is, by any measure, an extraordinary and riveting performance.
It is theatrical magic, and Mays never lets us down for a minute.

Fortunately, that actor is Tony Award-winner Jefferson Mays, who, as he demonstrated in I Am My Own Wife and A Gentleman's Guide to Murder, isn't content to play but one character when he can play many more.

Another holiday season, another take on 'A Christmas Carol.' Like other theatrical versions of the classic, this one ends with the same words credited to Tiny Tim...a production this taut and well-told is its own sort of blessing.
In this production conceived by director Michael Arden and designer Dane Laffrey, it gives new meaning to Theater with a capital T.
Opening tonight at Broadway’s Nederlander Theater, it’s still exceptional…in three ways.

The production continues to be worth watching, but the humbug curmudgeons in the audience might wonder if maybe, despite the show’s theme of stinginess, another actor or two could be hired to handle some of the lighter lifting of Dickens’ less indelible characters.
I feel a bit like Scrooge himself not to be fully embracing this production.

Given its loss of focus and overdose on sentiment, this Christmas Carol feels deflated by the time Scrooge finally awakes, and though Mays’ warm final words are something of a balm, the finale ultimately lands with a thud.
Without a solid, unbreakable connection between actor and audience, it becomes a display of theatrical craft for its own sake.

cn.t: Mays delivers a technically impressive solo performance across 50 characters, but critics split on whether the production's dark tone and dazzling effects overshadow the story's emotional core and Scrooge's transformation.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
